subject: ENGL
title: Colonial and Post-Colonial Literature in English
description: A critical examination of English-language poetry, fiction, drama and prose from former colonies and dependencies of the British empire. Special emphasis on defining the imperial and colonial experiences and on the literary legacy of British imperialism. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval.

subject: ENGL
title: Disability in Literature
description: Study of literary representations of disability, including general coverage of the different methodologies that can be used to assess such representations. subject: ENGL

title: Topics in Literature and the Environment

subject: ENGL
title: Reading Like A Writer: Young Adult
description: Designed to provide students with a context for the creation of their own work, this course explores the roots and evolution of forms in creative writing for young adults. subject: ENGL
title: Reading Like a Writer: The Short Lyric Tradition

Close attention will be paid to issues of craft, convention, and innovation. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval.

subject: ENGL
title: Reading Like a Writer: Creative NonFiction
description: Designed to provide students with a context for the creation of their own work, this course explores the roots and evolution of nonfictional forms in creative writing. Close attention will be paid to issues of craft, convention, and innovation. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval.

subject: ENGL
title: Creative Writing: Nonfiction

subject: ENGL
title: Creative Writing: Poetry

subject: ENGL
title: Creative Writing: Fiction

subject: ENGL
title: Multi-Genre Creative Writing Workshop

subject: ENGL
title: Literary Editing and Publishing
description: Practical experience in literary publishing through work on the Sequoya Review, the campus literary journal. subject: ENGL

subject: ENGL

description: This course examines the histories and social structures of East Asia from antiquity to 1600, with particular focus on China, Japan, and Korea. description: This course examines the emergence of modern nations from the rich and diverse cultures of East Asia and their transformations since 1600, with particular focus on China, Japan, and Korea. The course analyzes linkages within Asia and with other regions by focusing on how modernity, imperialism, and nationalism shaped each area and the region. Every 3-4 semesters.

subject: HIST
title: Inventing the Americas (CZ or HF)
description: This course explores the processes by which the Americas (North and South) were defined and constructed from the arrival of Europeans at the end of the 1400s up to the Wars of Independence that swept across both continents in the early 1800s. subject: HIST
title: Revolutionary Americas (CZ or HF)
description: This course begins with the Wars of Independence that engulfed Latin America in the early 1800s and continues up to the present day. description: The Middle East is one of the most important and complex areas of the world, and the region’s events and affairs have always been of international significance. description: A survey course that may cover comparative or regional histories or themes (such as religious, economic, or gender history) that centers on the United States. Prerequisites (if any) to be specified when the course topic is announced. On demand.

description: A survey course that may cover comparative or regional histories or themes (such as religious, economic, or gender history) that centers on Europe. Prerequisites (if any) to be specified when the course topic is announced. On demand.

title: Ancient Near East and Egypt
description: This course will explore both Ancient Egyptian and Near Eastern culture and geography to understand the foundations of these earliest civilizations and their impact on the ancient world. subject: HIST
title: Ancient Greece
description: A broad survey of the political, cultural, and social history of Ancient Greece. Topics may include Bronze Age culture, the Persian Wars, Classical Athens and Sparta, the rise of Macedonia, as well as the art, philosophy, and religion of Greece’s polis-based society. May be registered as CLAS 3110 . Credit not allowed in both HIST 3110 and CLAS 3110 .

subject: HIST
title: Ancient Rome
description: This course provides a broad survey of the political, cultural, and social history of Ancient Rome from its founding to its transformation in the fifth century C.E. Topics covered include art, philosophy, and literature; the rise of bureaucratic government; the Roman economy; and life under the emperors. May be registered as CLAS 3120 . Credit not allowed in both HIST 3120 and CLAS 3120 .

subject: HIST
title: Renaissance Culture and Society
description: An exploration of the rise of humanism in fourteenth-century Italy and the spread of humanistic ideas into greater Europe and the responses to it throughout high culture, religion, government, the sciences, and expansion abroad to ca. 1600.

subject: HIST
title: Reformation Europe and the World
description: A study of the religious, political, social, and economic factors involved in the Protestant and Catholic Reformations as well as their impact on European culture and continued religious reform through the end of the seventeenth century.

subject: HIST
title: Under Hitler’s Shadow: Europe 1929-1945
description: A comparative approach to the study of Europe from the outbreak of the economic depression in 1929 to the end of the second World War in 1945. subject: HIST
title: The Holocaust: Perpetrators, Victims, and Bystanders
description: This course is about the genocide of the Second World War known as the Holocaust. The focus will be on the people involved: the perpetrators, victims, and bystanders. subject: HIST
title: England to 1688
description: Upper-level survey examines important political, economic, social, and cultural developments, including the rise of English national identity, the development of Parliament, the Protestant Reformation, the English Civil Wars, the Restoration of the Monarchy, and the Glorious Revolution. Every 3-4 semesters.

subject: HIST
title: England since 1688
description: Upper-level survey examines important political, economic, social, and cultural developments, including England’s transition from a pre-modern to a modern society, the development of cabinet government, the rise and fall of the British Empire, the industrial revolution, and the question of Britain’s relative decline since World War II. Every 3-4 semesters.

subject: HIST
title: History of Modern Russia
description: This course surveys the history of Russia with emphasis on the modern period. Topics covered include imperialism, absolutism, the Enlightenment, industrialization and its impact, as well as the revolutions and rise of Soviet Russia.

subject: HIST
title: American Public History
description: American Public History introduces students to the practice of public history in its various forms as well as its methodological, theoretical, and ethical underpinnings. The course offers students opportunities to explore the diverse ways historians approach preserving and interpreting history and displaying historical research and topics to public audiences. On demand.

subject: HIST
title: American Sexual Histories
description: An examination of shifting perceptions of gender and sexuality over the course of United States history. Credit not allowed in both HIST 3420 and WGSS 3420 .

subject: HIST
title: Queer American History
description: While terms like gay, lesbian, bisexual, transgender, and intersex have relatively recent origins, the contemporary LGBTQ+ community has deep historical roots in America. title: Slavery in the Cities: Histories of Urban Enslavement
description: This course will examine the history of slavery in the colonial, early national, and antebellum United States, with emphasis on histories of urban enslavement in its various forms, contexts, and experiences. title: African American History to 1865
description: An exploration of the trials and triumphs that African Americans have experienced from colonial times to the Civil War; topics include the slave trade, the development of slave societies, the master-slave relationship, black culture, community, and resistance, and Emancipation.

subject: HIST

description: An exploration of the trials and triumphs that African Americans have experienced from Reconstruction to the present; topics include the Jim Crow era, the Great Migration, Civil Rights struggles, and black artistic and literary movements.

subject: HIST

description: This rotating selection of special topics courses focuses on the U. S. South. Every 3-4 semesters.

title: American Popular Culture
description: An exploration American history through the lens of popular culture, arts, and entertainments. Topics will include the development of American newspaper publishing, the early age of radio, escapist cinema in the Depression era, and the politics of popular music in the 1960s.

subject: HIST
title: The Modern Civil Rights Struggle
description: This course surveys the history of the modern civil rights movement by examining protests tactics, the impact of the Cold War, white mass resistance, and federal legislation; grassroots and charismatic leadership, and the political, cultural, transnational legacies of the movement.

subject: HIST
title: Topics in Urban History
description: This course explores the role the city plays in the history of a region within the instructor’s research speciality. Students will examine topics such as foundation of a city, city planning, expansion and contraction, municipal politics, social mores, city institutions, expression of identity and power through space and place, and other topics peculiar to urban history. On demand.

title: The Civil War in American Memory
description: Students will examine how Americans have reconstructed the memory of the Civil War to suit their needs and circumstances. subject: IARC
title: Design Fundamentals
description: A study of design as related to the individual and his or her environment; review of the basic theories including the elements and principles of design with emphasis on using design to solve utilitarian as well as aesthetic problems. Studio 6 hours. Open to Interior Architecture majors or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC

description: Develop techniques of volumetric study providing emphasis on design ideation through sketching and models. Studio 6 hours. Open to Interior Architecture majors or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

description: An introduction to architectural drafting including the study of symbols and drafting techniques necessary to the understanding and drawing of architectural plans. Studio 6 hours. Open to Interior Architecture majors or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC
title: Color Systems
description: Experimentation in color systems and their use in interior design; analysis of psychological impact of color systems on people; correlation of color scheme to total room design; development of skills for various media and tools used in color planning. Studio 6 hours. Open to Interior Architecture majors or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC
title: Survey of Architecture (HF)
description: An overview of architectural throughout history. Designed to heighten the student’s perception and appreciation of the role architecture has played in the development of society and culture. On demand.

subject: IARC

description: A field study of design and culture. On demand. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC
title: Special Projects
description: Individual or group projects. Maximum credit 4 hours. On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval.

description: Application of space planning techniques in small scale commercial and residential design; emphasis placed on human factors. Studio 6 hours. Corequisites: IARC 2050 or Department Head approval. Acceptance into Interior Architecture major or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC
title: Ideation and Visualization
description: An introduction to techniques for visual communication and idea generation that supports the design process. Studio 6 hours. Acceptance into Interior Architecture major or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

description: A study of the aesthetic and technical elements of kitchen and bath design with emphasis on NKBA standards. Studio 6 hours. Prerequisites: IARC 2000 and IARC 2050 with grades of C or better or Department Head approval. Corequisites: IARC 2220 or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC
title: Computer Applications in Design
description: Introduction to digital software applications for the creation of graphic presentations, portfolios, and digital illustrations. Lecture 3 hours. Acceptance into Interior Architecture major or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC
title: Interior Materials
description: A study of basic components used in the art of interior design: wall treatments, window treatments, floor coverings, fabric selections, furniture selections. Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Interior Architecture major or Department Head approval.

subject: IARC
title: Interior Textiles
description: A study of the fundamental properties found in textile fibers, yarns, weaves and finishes, and the application of these properties to interior finishes. Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Interior Architecture major or Department Head approval.

subject: IARC
title: Computer-Aided Design 1
description: Introduction to the fundamentals of two dimensional (2d) computer drafting using AutoCad. Develop the requisite skills for implementing various basic commands needed to create presentation drawings, working drawings and details. Studio 5 hours. Prerequisites: IARC 1100 with a grade of C or better or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC

description: Advanced study of residential space planning criteria and the selection of furnishings, equipment, materials, and finishes for the residential market; design considerations for special populations (e.g., disabled, aged) explored. Studio 6 hours. Prerequisites: IARC 3000 and IARC 3150 with grades of C or better or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC
title: Building Information Modeling
description: Introduction to REVIT developing two dimensional (2D) and three dimensional (3D) computer drafting skills and the creation of construction documents and presentation drawings. Studio 6 hours. Prerequisites: IARC 1100 and IARC 2100 with grades of C or better or Department Head approval. Laboratory/studio course fee will be assessed.

subject: IARC

description: The study of design characteristics of historical architecture, interiors, furniture and decorative arts including the dominant, socio-economic influences leading to the development of each style – Egyptian to Victorian. Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Interior Architecture major or Department Head approval.

subject: IARC

description: The study of design characteristics of historical architecture, interiors, furniture and decorative arts including effects of the Industrial Revolution - Victorian to Modern. Prerequisites: IARC 3200 with a grade of C or better or Department Head approval.

subject: IARC

description: A comprehensive survey, period feature-by-feature, of the styles that have had the greatest impact on the development of American architecture.

subject: MUS

subject: MUS
title: Orchestration

title: Choral Conducting
description: Designed to teach the student to train choral groups, read choral scores, and conduct effective rehearsals; basic patterns for choral and orchestral conducting, interpretation and building of repertoire of both secular and sacred choral composition. Actual conducting of works of all periods with and without instrumental accompaniment. Spring semester. Prerequisites: MUS 2710 , MUS 2720 and MUS 303

subject: MUS
title: Musics of the World (CZ or HF)
description: An introduction to the folk and ethnic music of various world cultures. Consideration of how musical styles relate to social, cultural and aesthetic practices and attitudes. Spring semester. May be registered as HUM 3110 . Credit not allowed in both MUS 3110 and HUM 3110 .

subject: MUS
title: America’s Musical Heritage (HF)
description: An historical study of the origins and impacts of American musical traditions, including music of diverse cultures, regions, and communities; focuses on the contributions of native peoples, African Americans, and immigrants. The impact of recording and video technologies is also explored. Fall and Spring semesters.

subject: MUS

description: A general survey of the history of music in western civilization. Fall semester. Prerequisites: MUS 1720 or Department Head approval.

subject: MUS
title: History of Music 2
description: A general survey of the history of music in western civilization. Spring semester. Prerequisites: MUS 1720 or Department Head approval.

subject: MUS
title: Survey of Jazz (HF)
description: A introductory survey course in jazz from its ethnic origins, through its chronological development, to its current styles. Emphasis placed on the relationship of the music to the individuals who create this form of human expression. Every semester. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval.

subject: MUS
title: African American Music: An Introduction (HF)
description: An overview of vocal and instrumental genres rooted in the African American experience, spotlighting African American contributions from slavery to the present. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval.

subject: MUS
title: Elementary School Music Methods, Materials, and Observation
description: A study of music teaching-learning methods and strategies. Basic concepts of musical organization, musical skills, and literature for the classroom. Fall semester. Prerequisites: Piano Proficiency Exam or Department Head approval.

subject: MUS
title: Classroom Music Methods

subject: MUS

title: Choral Arranging

Prerequisites: MUS 2710 , MUS 2720 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS
title: American Politics (CZ or SB)
description: The foundations, institutions, processes and policies of American national government with attention to the Constitution and such topics as elections, political and civil rights and liberties, federalism, public policy, public opinion, political culture, interest groups, and the role of citizens in governance.

subject: PSPS
title: World Politics (CZ or SB)
description: The evolution, nature, and operation of the contemporary world political system with attention to the behavior of states, the impact of ideology, culture, and domestic politics on foreign policy, the behavior of transnational political and economic actors, the effects of international competition, and the impact of international institutions on promoting cooperation.

subject: PSPS
title: Controversies in Public Policy (SB)
description: Contemporary policy issues in American politics with attention to current problems, proposed solutions, and competing viewpoints.

subject: PSPS
title: Global Culture and Politics (CZ)
description: A study of culture, politics, and society in the non-western world with emphasis on significant intellectual contributions, modes of inquiry, value systems, structures of belief and practices of everyday life.

subject: PSPS
title: The First Year Experience in Political Science
description: An introduction to the college experience for first-year students at UTC and the aspects needed for a successful transition from high school to college. subject: PSPS
title: American Political Thought
description: A study of the major political and constitutional ideas that have influenced the development of the United States since its founding. Recommended for pre-law majors.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

description: Tennessee state and local government and politics with comparisons to government and politics in the other states.

subject: PSPS
title: The Presidency
description: An examination of the origins and historical development of the American presidency, the institutional context of presidential leadership, and the concept of presidential power.

subject: PSPS

description: An examination of the U.S. Congress, the legislative process, and the institution’s relationship with other political actors, including such key themes as deliberation, policymaking, representation, transparency, and leadership.

subject: PSPS
title: Introduction to Judicial Process
description: An examination of the role, operation and decision-making processes of the U.S. Supreme Court and lower federal courts. Recommended for pre-law majors.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS
title: Public Policy Theory

subject: PSPS
title: Introduction to Public Administration
description: Introduction to the concepts and practices of Public Administration. Designed to give students understanding of public sector administration. This course provides an overview of traditional and contemporary views of public administration.

subject: PSPS
title: Introduction to Nonprofit Sector
description: Introduction to the nonprofit and voluntary sector in the United States. Examines issues and theories about the existence, forms, and functions of the Nonprofit Sector. Provides an overview of history and modern developments of the Nonprofit Sector.

subject: PSPS
title: Comparative Government (CZ or SB)
description: An examination of how different societies can be compared and contrasted, with a focus on transformation.

subject: PSPS
title: International Relations
description: An examination of the theoretical, historical and behavioral causes of war and peace. Focus on the role of power, sovereignty, and international law on world politics.

subject: PSPS
title: Political Sociology
description: Discusses the social organization of political power and how society affects politics and the state, exploring the social dimensions of power and political institutions. Key topics includes elites, social classes, the state, the media, social movements and related organizations, seminal events, and theories that have informed the resulting politics.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

description: This course is designed to assist students as they prepare to embark on future career opportunities in political science, public administration, public policy, and nonprofit careers. Students will learn to research job opportunities, prepare career professional materials, network, and conduct professional interviews. Open only to Political Science and Public Service majors.

subject: PSPS

description: An introduction to such theoretical concerns of Western political science as sovereignty, rights, justice, property, liberty, and equality. This course emphasizes the ancient philosophers through the Enlightenment, such as given in the works of Sophocles, Plato, Aristotle, through Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau.

subject: PSPS
title: Modern Political Philosophy (HF)
description: An introduction to such theoretical concerns of Western political science as sovereignty, rights, justice, property, liberty, and equality. This course emphasizes more contemporary philosophers, such as given in the works of Mill, Marx, and Nietzsche, through the twentieth century, to current arguments regarding liberty, equality, and fairness.

subject: PSPS
title: Contemporary Political Ideas
description: Focuses upon contemporary perspectives in political and social thought with an emphasis on competing world views.

subject: PSPS

description: A general overview of the media and American politics, with a focus on the role the media play in American politics, in mediating messages to the public, and in influencing political attitudes and political behavior. Rather, it serves as an introduction to the broad theme of political communication.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS
title: American Political Development
description: An introduction to the subfield of American political development (APD). Blending approaches in political science, history, and policy, APD identifies key historical patterns and tensions in American political life, revealing connections between the past and present.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS
title: Civil Liberties

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS
title: Special Topics in Public Policy

subject: PSPS

description: Examination of policy making and policy in the United States. Prerequisites: PSPS 2450 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSPS
title: Urban Public Policy
description: An introduction to the different approaches, ideas and programs advanced to address public policy urban problems.

subject: PSPS

description: This course emphasizes issues and skills development in public management, including administration, financial management, leadership/management of employees, performance measurement, ethics, and organizational behavior.

subject: PSPS

description: This course examines historical and emerging issues facing volunteer management programs in nonprofit organizations. The course will focus on recruitment and retention strategies, volunteer motivation, risk management and liability issues, application/screening procedures, and ethical issues facing nonprofits and volunteers.

subject: PSPS
title: Special Topics in Area Studies
description: The study of the governmental structures, processes, and ideologies of different regions of the world, comparing their political, economic, and social policies. May be repeated to focus on different regions of the world.

subject: PSPS
title: Comparative Public Policy
description: The formation and implementation of public policies in different countries of the world.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS
title: Politics of Immigration
description: An examination of immigration policy in the United States and internationally, with an emphasis on historical patterns, policy debates, legal ramifications, and domestic and international migration regulations and agencies.

subject: PSPS
title: Religion and Politics in a Globalized World
description: Impact of religion on politics and the reverse, exploring the relationship between religion and global politics, the impact of modernization, and its salience in contemporary political life.

subject: PSPS
title: Group Studies
description: On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval. Department may have additional prerequisite requirements.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

Prerequisites: PSPS 3000 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

Prerequisites: PSPS 3000 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

subject: PSPS

description: Internship in a public agency or nonprofit organization providing students the opportunity to integrate and extend classroom learning with practice. No more than 3 credit hours may apply toward the major degree requirements. 50 on site hours per credit hour. Prerequisites: Minimum 2.75 cumulative grade point average and prior approval of Department Head. Junior standing.

description: Supervised internship in a public or nonprofit organization related to a student’s academic and career goals. Students must apply to the PANM advisor for admission to field placement. description: Introduction to contemporary psychology as a basic and applied social science; analysis of biological, mental, and social determinants of human behavior from the standpoint of psychological theory, research, and practice. Every semester.

subject: PSY
title: Special Projects
description: Individual or group projects. Maximum credit 4 hours. On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Introductory Statistics in Psychology (QR)
description: Descriptive and inferential statistics with computer analysis of data from psychological and other social sciences. Traditional and modern descriptive techniques, correlation and regression analysis, probability concepts, inferential techniques on means through analysis of variance, power analysis, and selected nonparametric techniques are presented. subject: PSY
title: Research Methods in Psychology
description: General introduction to research methods in psychology with an emphasis on basic strategies for empirically identifying causal and correlational relationships. Topics will include laboratory and field techniques, quasi-experimental and non-experimental models, and the ethical issues involved in research. Every semester. Lecture 3 hours, laboratory 1 hour. subject: PSY

description: Tutorial and laboratory exercises to help students master use of professional quality computer software to solve statistical problems. Prerequisites: Math ACT subscore of 22 (SAT 520) or higher or any approved general education mathematics course or Department Head approval. Pre or Corequisites: PSY 2010 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology as a Profession
description: Role modeling of the psychological practitioner in diverse professional contexts. Discussion of the foundations, methods, ethics, legal issues, and relationships with other specialists involved in professional psychology. Required for psychology majors. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 and Psychology major or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Lifespan Development
description: Comprehensive, contemporary, research-oriented treatment of human development from infancy through late adulthood. Topics include physical, intellectual, emotional, and social development and the interactions between these domains. Applications to family, work and other contexts will be examined. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: The Psychology of Child Development
description: Infancy through childhood. Concepts of development and functioning derived from research and observation. Emphasis on the roles of both biological and experiential factors in physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development. Child-rearing applications. Every semester. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 or Department Head approval. Credit not allowed in both EDUC 2030 and PSY 2210.

subject: PSY
title: The Psychology of Adolescence and Adulthood
description: Principles of adolescent functionality. Evaluation of various theories of adolescence. Psychodynamic consideration of life-span development concepts and the adjustment problems related to aging. Emphasis on age-related changes. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 or Department Head approval. Credit not allowed in both EDUC 2420 and PSY 2220.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Aging
description: Theoretical and empirical introduction to the psychological development of older adults. Discussion of cognition, personality, social behavior, and sensor motor changes as they evolve at the adult end of the life span. Examination of psychological issues in adult coping, death and dying, and work and family roles. On demand. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Individual Differences
description: Develops an understanding of the most difficult aspect of human behavior to comprehend: differences. Investigating the three major causes of differences. Exploring the implications the course perspective has for personal, educational

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Black Experience
description: Impact of cultural differences from a psychological perspective. Principles, theories, and research in psychology applied to black experience. Differences in socialization, personality, and social processes. Topics include intelligence, racial identity, and psycholinguistics. Every semester.

subject: PSY
title: Group Studies
description: On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval. Department may have additional prerequisite requirements.

subject: PSY
title: Psychopathology
description: A biosocial approach to theories of causation, development, and symptomatic behavior in emotional disorder; theoretical bases of the various therapies and of positive means of prevention. Every semester. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 and 3 additional hours of psychology or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Learning and Motivation
description: Study of the effective conditions for various learning phenomena; roles of motivation, reinforcement, and punishment in learning. Prerequisites: PSY 2020 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Sensation and Perception
description: Study of sensory and perceptual processes; examination of the sense organs and related neurophysiological mechanisms, and the necessary stimulus conditions for particular perceptual phenomena. Prerequisites: PSY 2020 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Cognitive Science
description: Examination of the ways in which people process information; with an emphasis on attention, memory, problem-solving, and language. Every semester. Prerequisites: PSY 2020 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Biological Psychology
description: The study of the physiological bases of behavior with emphasis on the functional neural systems of the brain which mediate behavior. Course content is designed to familiarize students with basic neuroanatomy and neurophysiological techniques used in the investigation of brain functions and behavior. Fall semester. Prerequisites: PSY 2020 or 6 hours of college biology courses, or Department Head ap

subject: PSY
title: Principles of Neuropsychology
description: Comprehensive examination of the history, methodological approaches and applications associated with neuropsychology. Emphasis will be placed on the functional impact of changes to the brain and how those changes are commonly assessed. Prerequisites: PSY 2020 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Health and Illness: Socio-Cultural Perspectives
description: The sociocultural study of medicine, illness, and disease; including the development of medicine and medical care, non-Western medical systems, health disparities, cultural beliefs about illness, and the social construction of illness. Prerequisites: ANTH 1200 or SOC 1510 or Department Head approval. May be registered as SOC 3650 or ANTH 3220 . Credit allowed in only one of the three courses.

subject: PSY
title: Drugs and Behavior
description: In this course, you will be introduced to the field of substance use and misuse across the lifespan. The first portion of this course will cover the history of drugs and substance use behaviors, pharmacology of drugs, neurobiology of addiction, and development and maintenance of use. The second portion of the course will cover specific drugs, focusing on alcohol and prescription medication misuse,

subject: PSY
title: Social Psychology
description: Survey of the general concepts and research areas in social psychology. Emphasis upon the interactions between the individual and society with consideration of such topics as attitudes, prejudices, conformity, deviance, socialization, and interpersonal attraction. Every semester. Prerequisites: 6 hours of psychology or sociology or Department Head approval. May be registered for as SOC 3310 . Cred

subject: PSY
title: Positive Psychology
description: This course is an evidence-based approach to the positive possibilities in our adult lives. Key words for the course are well-being, meaningfulness, interest, efficacy, positive regard, optimism, flow, love and happiness. subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Human Sexuality
description: This course will introduce the study of human sexuality. Specifically, this course investigates human sexuality from biological and psychological perspectives. We will study male, female, and intersex sexual anatomy; sexual arousal, sexual response, and behaviors; gender identity and sexual orientation; and communication in relationships. subject: PSY
title: Applied Developmental Psychology
description: An in depth examination of interactions among 1) processes in cognitive, language, social, and emotional development and 2) environmental experiences of children, from birth through adolescence. Emphasis on analysis of the implications of these interactions for the welfare of current and future generations of children. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 ; PSY 2210 or PSY 2220 or EDUC 2420 or ECHD 2430 ; or D

subject: PSY
title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
description: Principles of psychological measurements including reliability, validity, errors of measurement, techniques of test construction, and problems in assessment and prediction. Laboratory use of selected tests. Fall semester. Prerequisites: PSY 1010 , PSY 2010 , PSY 2020 , and PSY 2040 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Fieldwork/Research/Service Learning in Applied Psychology
description: Program provides students with practical experience in an organization or facility related to psychology. Students are provided opportunities to gain experience in a supervised role, with responsibilities that are relevant to psychology. It is designed to enhance student learning and to guide students in their decisions on what to do with a psychology degree. Enrollment is by permission of instruc

subject: PSY
title: Practicum in Teaching Psychology
description: A practicum providing students the opportunity to gain teaching experience, enhance their knowledge of a particular area in psychology, and acquire professional skills that make them more competitive for graduate school and in the job market. Prerequisites: PSY 2020 and Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Modern Psychological Studies
description: Modern Psychological Studies is a journal that publishes undergraduate research in psychology. Students in this course serve as the editorial board for the journal and critique, edit, and decide if a submission to MPS will be published. subject: PSY
title: Psychology Camp Training
description: This course provides students the knowledge, tools and information to better prepare them for a practicum related to individuals with a variety of disabilities, focusing on summer service camps for Camp Zooability and the Creative Discovery Museum.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Culture, Ethnicity, and Race
description: Survey of the general concepts and research areas in culture, ethnicity, and race within the field of psychology. Emphasis upon the interactions between culture and psychological concepts such as cognition, language, gender, behaviors, and health and intergroup relations. On demand. Prerequisites: Prerequisite: 6 credit hours of psychology courses OR 6 credit hours of sociology courses OR Departme

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Language
description: An examination of the ways in which humans acquire, use, and comprehend language; emphasis on the role of biological and social development, cognitive processes, and the impact of culture on linguistic skills.Every semester. Lecture 3 hours.Prerequisites: PSY 1010 , PSY 2010 or equivalent, PSY 2020 , and PSY 2040 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology Abroad
description: The focus of this 14-day study abroad course is to learn about important people and events in the history of Psychology. subject: PSY

description: On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval. Department may have additional prerequisite requirements.

title: Industrial/Organizational Psychology
description: Introduction to the study of organizations with emphasis upon personnel selection, criteria, and training. Special consideration of work motivation, job satisfaction, and the role of the organization in behavior. Every semester. Prerequisites: 6 hours of psychology or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Contemporary Psychotherapies
description: A comprehensive review of psychotherapeutic techniques practiced to help alleviate individuals’ behavioral, cognitive, and emotional disabilities. Reviews practices derived from the behavioral, cognitive, humanistic, psychodynamic perspectives. In addition, the course emphasizes the empirical research demonstrating the efficacy of these techniques. Prerequisites: 6 hours of psychology and PSY 3080

subject: PSY
title: Advanced Seminar for Psychological Processes
description: A comprehensive review of the field as summary experience, especially for senior major students planning to enter graduate study. Prerequisites: 15 hours of psychology including PSY 2020 and senior standing, or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Topics in Advanced Cognitive Psychology
description: The purpose of this course is to provide an understanding of human memory function from an experimental psychology perspective. subject: PSY

description: Intensive treatment of selected research areas in biological psychology. Emphasis upon the interrelationship between current theoretical perspectives and appropriate methodological procedures. Prerequisites: 6 hours of psychology including 3 credits in PSY 3120 or PSY 3140 or PSY 3180 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Health Psychology
description: This course provides a framework for understanding human health from biopsychosocial perspective, acknowledging the interplay between biological, social, and psychological factors affecting the onset and prognosis of various health-related conditions. subject: PSY
title: Psychology and Law
description: A comprehensive review of how psychological theory and research influences social policy and law. subject: PSY
title: Topics in Advanced Social Psychology
description: Intensive treatment of selected research areas in social psychology. Emphasis upon the interrelationship between current theoretical perspectives and appropriate methodological procedures. On demand. Prerequisites: PSY 3310 or Department Head approval. May be registered as SOC 4310R .

subject: PSY
title: Topics in Advanced Developmental Psychology
description: Intensive treatment of selected topic areas in developmental psychology. Emphasis upon the interrelationships between current theoretical perspectives and appropriate methodological procedures. Prerequisites: 6 hours in psychology including 3 credits in PSY 2210 or PSY 2220 or PSY 2230 or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Men and Masculinities
description: This course centers on the lived experiences of men and boys. This course explores diverse theoretical models (i.e., biopsychosocial models, feminist perspectives, intersectional frameworks) on the development and psychological experiences of men/masculinity. This course also discusses psychological experiences and outcomes of men and masculinity as they relate to topics such as mental and physica

subject: PSY
title: Theories of Personality
description: Survey of basic theories of personality including the psychoanalytic, sociocultural, factor analytic, the biosocial, and the phenomenological. Strongly suggested for guidance majors. Prerequisites: 6 hours of psychology or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Psychology of Women
description: Analysis of empirical data and theoretical viewpoints concerning the psychological development of women. Psychological effects of sex roles, achievement motivation, and abilities of women; models of socialization practices, personality development, and stages of adjustment. Fall semester. Prerequisites: 6 hours of psychology and junior standing or Department Head approval. May be registered as WGS

subject: PSY
title: Systems of Psychology
description: The historical development, major theses, elements of strength, shortcomings, and current trends of the principal schools of psychological thought. Reading and discussion course for psychology majors and graduate students. Every semester. Prerequisites: 15 hours of psychology and senior standing, or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY
title: Philosophical Psychology
description: Critical analysis of philosophical aspects of current systems of psychology. Particular focus upon assumptions and consequences of various modes of explanation and description. Fall semester. Prerequisites: 15 hours of psychology and senior standing, or Department Head approval.

subject: PSY

description: Analysis of empirical data and psychological theories involving religious beliefs, practices, and experiences. On demand. description: This course introduces the history and current status of public health, the legal basis of public health and how policy affects health, the structure and function of the public health system and sectors/programs of public health practice, and social and behavioral interventions designed to improve the health status of a community.

subject: PUBH
title: Community Health
description: Interrelationship studies involving home, public health, non-official organizations/agencies for improved public health and health care delivery. Prerequisites: Completion of the General Education Behavioral and Social Science category and a minimum 2.5 overall GPA or Department Head approval.

subject: PUBH
title: Introduction to Epidemiology (NL)
description: This course provides a general introduction to epidemiological concepts and methods in the study of public health. subject: PUBH

description: This course introduces the study and use of communication strategies to inform and influence decisions and actions to improve health. Applied examples of health communication and social marketing practices will be used throughout the course, along with an opportunity for students to develop their own health communication strategy.Prerequisites: A minimum 2.5 overall GPA or Department Head approval

subject: REL
title: Introduction to the Study of Religion (HF)
description: Consideration of the various elements of religion and the methods for studying them; attention to beliefs, world-views, and sacred literature; rituals, myths, symbols; religious communities and organizations; types of religious experience. Every semester.

subject: REL

description: An introduction to global Islamic traditions that focuses on key Muslim histories, the Qur’an, diverse religious practices, arts and architecture, and legal and theological traditions. Considers contemporary issues from a global perspective, including attitudes towards gender and sexuality, unity and diversity in the community, and the problem of Islamophobia.

subject: REL
title: Buddhism: Teachings, Practices, and Socio-cultural History (CZ or HF)
description: Introduction to the core beliefs, values, practices, and history of all three major Buddhist traditions: Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana. The life of the Buddha, Buddhist suttas/sutras, fundamental concepts of karma & rebirth, the Four Noble Truths, nibbana/nirvana, emptiness, etc. Core practices of meditation, devotionalism, and chanting. subject: REL
title: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam (HF)
description: An introduction to the major religious traditions emerging in Western cultures, with emphasis on Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Fall and Spring semesters.

subject: REL
title: Special Projects
description: Individual or group projects. Maximum credit 4 hours. On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval.

subject: REL
title: Religions of Asia (CZ or HF)
description: An introduction to the major religious traditions of Asia, including Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism, and Confucianism. Spring semester.

subject: REL
title: A History of Judaism (HF)
description: Examination of enduring themes or concepts in Jewish tradition from antiquity to the modern era. Particular attention to the emergence of normative Judaism and its later challengers: Hasidism, Reform, and Zionism. Fall semester.

subject: REL
title: The History of Christianity (HF)
description: An introduction to historical Christianity, including the major personalities, events, and theological themes, from the New Testament period to the present.

subject: REL
title: Biblical Literature I: Old Testament (HF)
description: The Old Testament and the history and religion of Israel against the background of the ancient Near East. Fall semester.

subject: REL
title: Biblical Literature II: New Testament (HF)
description: The New Testament documents in relation to Judaism and the environment of the Hellenistic world. Spring semester.

subject: REL
title: Topics in Popular Culture, Philosophy, and Religion (HF)
description: An introduction to the study of philosophy and/or religious studies through popular culture. title: Religion in American Life (HF)
description: Attention to distinctly American phenomena, with the intention of assessing the present role and status of religion; consideration of such topics as separation of church and state, revivalism, the influence of immigration, sects, and cults. Fall semester.

title: The History of American Evangelicalism (HF)
description: This course examines the history of evangelicalism, from its roots in the late 17 th century to the present. Special attention is given to evangelicalism in its American form as well as leading figures of the movement, such as Jonathan Edwards, John Wesley, Charles Spurgeon, D. L. Moody, and Billy Graham. Every other semester.

subject: REL

description: Exploration of the religious beliefs, practices, and religious specialists of primary religions, such as, magic (spells, mantras, witchcraft, amulets, etc.), divination (astrology, palm reading, number systems, cards, I-Ching, etc.), and magic-religious specialists (shamans, spirit mediums, witches, fortunetellers, etc.). subject: REL
title: The Qur’an
description: An introduction to the Qur’an, the primary scripture of the Islamic religious tradition. This course focuses on themes in the Qur’an and its history, the text’s style and poetics, practices of recitation, the Qur’an as a source of law and theology, and the relationship of the text to contemporary debates on politics, gender justice, and Muslim sexualities.

subject: REL
title: American Islamic Traditions: History and Practice From The Slave Trade to Today
description: This course explores American Islamic traditions and focuses on key histories, diverse religious practices, and major aspects of debates in contemporary American Muslim communities. Students will learn theories of religion and society and apply them in analysis of historical and current American Muslim viewpoints. subject: REL
title: Modern Judaism
description: Exploration of religious, social, and political developments in modern Judaism, including the appearance of Zionism, the impact of the Holocaust, and efforts to overcome the tension between Zionism and the religious culture of contemporary Jews. Alternate years.

subject: REL
title: Religions of India
description: Examination of the conceptual and historical development of religions on the Indian subcontinent. Attention will also be paid to the interaction among religions of India and their relationships to Indian culture. Alternate years.

subject: REL
title: Religions of China
description: Examination of the conceptual and historical development of religions in China. Attention will also be paid to the interaction among religions of China, the impact of Indian religions and culture on China, and the relationship of religion to Chinese culture. Alternate years.

subject: REL
title: Philosophy of Religion
description: A philosophical examination of religion, including traditional and modern arguments for the existence and nature of God, the nature of religious experience and belief, and the functions of religious language. Alternate years. May be registered as PHIL 3330 . Credit not allowed in both REL 3330 and PHIL 3330 .

subject: REL
title: Religion in Southern Culture
description: Examination of the role of religion in Southern culture, past and present. Attention to the evangelical influence, African-American religion, mountain religion, Southern-based sects, the Pentecostal experience, and the cultural impact of religion in the South. Alternate years.

subject: REL

description: The development of central issues in Christian thought in the first millennium, with an emphasis on how these emerged from a historical context as responses both to the demands of faith and to the social and intellectual concerns of the time. Consideration of such figures as Tertullian, Arius, Augustine, Gregory the Great, and Bede. Alternate years.

subject: REL
title: Medieval Philosophy
description: This course will trace the development of philosophy from late Antiquity through the High Middle Ages. Texts will be drawn from medieval Christian, Jewish, or Muslim authors. May be registered as PHIL 3520 . Credit not allowed in both REL 3520 and PHIL 3520 .

subject: REL
title: Modern Christian Thought
description: Selected movements and figures that have shaped the Christian theological tradition in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Alternate years.

subject: REL
title: The Roots of Methodism and Evangelicalism in America and Europe
description: This course is a study of the origin of Methodism and evangelicalism in eighteenth-century America and Europe. Particular attention is given to the leading figures of the transatlantic revivals and their contribution to Methodism and evangelicalism. Every other Spring semester. Lecture 3 hours.

subject: REL
title: Jonathan Edwards’s Life, Thought, and Legacy in American Religious Culture
description: This course is a study of Jonathan Edwards’s life, theology, and legacy as it pertains to American religious culture. Spring semester.

subject: REL
title: Death or Glory: Religion and War
description: Study of the intertwining of military ideals and spirit with religious belief and practice. Examination of scriptural passages on war. Survey of ethics of war from diverse religious traditions, framed, in part, by pacifist, militarist, realist and just war traditions and International Humanitarian Law. subject: REL
title: The Faiths of the Founding Fathers (and Mothers)
description: This course is a study of the religious beliefs of the Founding Fathers (and Mothers) in America. Particular attention is given to religion in America and the role of the Founders in establishing the separation of church and state. Spring semester.

title: Gender and Sexuality in Religion
description: How do ideas about gender and sexuality offer new ways to understand religion, society, and culture? subject: REL
title: Mysticism East and West
description: The place of mysticism in the Eastern and Western religious traditions; discussion of the writings of major historical and contemporary mystics. On demand.

description: Analysis of selected issues, such as church-state relations, fundamentalism, and debates over abortion, that are central to contemporary religious life. Primary attention to the American scene and some cross-cultural comparisons. Alternate years.

description: Examination of the Holocaust, the state-sponsored effort of the Nazi regime to destroy the Jewish people between 1933 and 1945, and the relationship between the Holocaust and the more general category of genocide. Prerequisites: Department Head approval.

A multi-disciplinary teaching context with focus on women’s self identity, women’s identity in families, and women’s identity in society. Prerequisites: ENGL 1010 or ENGL 1011 or UHON 1010 or Department Head approval.

subject: WGSS
title: Women’s Issues in South Asia
description: A survey of contemporary issues for women in South Asia. On demand.

subject: WGSS
title: Women’s Health Issues (CZ or SB)
description: A review of current literature and discussion of issues affecting contemporary women’s health. The course will introduce the biological, psychological, social, economic, and cultural factors which affect the health of women. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval. Open to non-majors.

subject: WGSS
title: Popular Fiction
description: Science fiction or detective fiction or other type of popular fiction, one or another of which will be studied for its literary merit: the type of popular fiction to be studied in any particular section will be specified in the schedule of classes. On demand. May be registered as ENGL 2510R.

subject: WGSS
title: Read, Write, Respawn
description: In this course, students will engage rhetorical theory and/or literary theory to analyze and create both traditional texts and video games. Fall and Spring semesters. May be registered as ENGL 2550.

subject: WGSS
title: Gender Based Violence (SB)
description: Examines a variety of forms of violence against women in the United States including domestic violence, sexual assault, sexual harassment and pornography. Explores how violence against women has been minimized in society and how the criminal justice system has rarely developed effective ways to address these types of crimes. May be registered as CRMJ 2950 . Credit not allowed in both CRMJ 2950 and

subject: WGSS
title: Group Studies
description: On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval. Department may have additional prerequisite requirements.

subject: WGSS
title: Latin American Women Writers in Translation
description: Contributions of Latin American women writers to the social, economic, and political institutions of Latin American culture. Readings from literary selections in several genres. Topics will include gender roles, systems of authority, masculine/feminine representations of reality, and the concept of “feminine” writing. No foreign language credit. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL 1010 or ENGL 1011 or

subject: WGSS
title: Gender and Society
description: Analysis of how ideas about gender are socially constructed and the importance of women-centered theories on this approach; the interplay of gender and various social structures including education, religion, politics, family, health, work and sexuality. Prerequisites: SOC 1150 or SOC 1510 with a minimum grade of C or Department Head approval. May be registered as SOC 3070 . Credit not allowed in

subject: WGSS
title: Women and Criminal Justice
description: This course is intended to provide an overview of women’s involvement in the criminal justice system as offenders, victims and professionals. Considerable attention will be given to women as victims of crime, the social system and the criminal justice process. On demand. Prerequisites: CRMJ 1100 or completion of social science general education requirement or Department Head approval. May be regis

subject: WGSS
title: American Women Writers
description: A survey of American women writers of the 20th century. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval. May be registered as ENGL 3210 . Credit not allowed in both ENGL 3210 and WGSS 3210.

subject: WGSS
title: Race, Gender and the Media
description: Examines U.S. mass media construction of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality within an historical context and investigates the role of women and minority groups in U.S. media industries. On demand. Lecture 3 hours. Prerequisites: Department Head approval. Junior standing. May be registered as COMM 3240 . Credit not allowed in both COMM 3240 and WGSS 3240.

subject: WGSS
title: Economics of Gender, Race and Inequality
description: This course will explore how inequality is measured in society, its primary economic drivers, and its ultimate consequences. Outcome differences in variables such as education, employment, income, and wealth, will be measured across gender, race, nationality, and sexual orientation. How individual’s choices, constraints, and subjected discrimination can affect their economic outcomes will be analy

subject: WGSS
title: Gender in Politics
description: An examination of the role and status of women in the American political system. Special emphasis given to the impact of selected public policies upon women. On demand. May be registered as PSPS 3230 . Credit not allowed in both PSPS 3230 and WGSS 3360.

subject: WGSS
title: Psychology of Human Sexuality
description: This course will introduce the study of human sexuality. Specifically, this course investigates human sexuality from biological and psychological perspectives. We will study male, female, and intersex sexual anatomy; sexual arousal, sexual response, and behaviors; gender identity and sexual orientation; and communication in relationships. In addition, we will study contraception, sexual infections

subject: WGSS
title: American Sexual Histories
description: An examination of shifting perceptions of gender and sexuality over the course of United States history. Topics include ideas about interracial romance, sex censorship, the eugenics movement, the development of LGBT identities, shifting marital and familial norms and the development of feminist thought. May be registered as HIST 3420 . Credit not allowed in both WGSS 3420 and HIST 3420 .

subject: WGSS
title: Queer American History
description: While terms like gay, lesbian, bisexual, transgender, and intersex have relatively recent origins, the contemporary LGBTQ+ community has deep historical roots in America. Spanning from the seventeenth century to the present, this course explores the past experiences of individuals and groups who would be categorized today under the LGBTQ+ umbrella. It examines the long history of protest and polit

subject: WGSS
title: British Women Writers
description: A survey of British women writers with an eye to traditions, themes, and styles. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval. May be registered as ENGL 3450 . Credit not allowed in both WGSS 3450 and ENGL 3450 .

subject: WGSS
title: Group Studies
description: On demand. Prerequisites: Department Head approval. Department may have additional prerequisite requirements.

subject: WGSS
title: Theatre and Feminism
description: Readings, discussion and writing about a wide variety of plays by modern feminist playwrights. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or UHON 1020 or Department Head approval. May be registered as ENGL 4020 or THSP 4020 . Credit allowed in only one of the three courses.

subject: WGSS
title: Women, Gender, and Power in European History
description: A survey of the history of women and gender in medieval and early modern Europe. Topics will include pre-modern ideas about gender and women; gender in European empires; women’s role in and relationship to religion; men’s and women’s positions within the household; the regulation of sexuality; and the emergence of women’s rights. May be registered as HIST 4150 . Credit not allowed in both HIST 415

subject: WGSS
title: Gender and Sexuality in Religion
description: How do ideas about gender and sexuality offer new ways to understand religion, society, and culture? In this course we explore the diversity of sexual difference in context of contemporary global religions, especially Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism. Course themes include: the tension between theory and practice, authority and gender, women’s lives, masculinities, gender fluidity, and the role of th

subject: WGSS
title: Technologies of Sex and Gender
description: Synthesizing and applying sociological theories of technology, gender, and sexualities, this course explores how gender and sexuality are shaped by technology and science, affecting individual, group, and institutional norms, behaviors and processes. Salient topics such as digitized intimacy, gendered and sexual technoscience, and application of Artificial Intelligence to gendered processes will b

subject: WGSS
title: Gender and Law
description: An examination of the development of the legal definitions of gender in the United States, specifically centering on the tensions that occur in a democratic system when disenfranchised groups seek power, with attention to the role that the law and legal structures play in the pursuit of equality. Prerequisites: PSPS 3000 or Department Head approval. May be registered as PSPS 4310 . Credit not allo

subject: WGSS
title: Psychology of Men and Masculinities
description: This course centers on the lived experiences of men and boys. This course explores diverse theoretical models (i.e., biopsychosocial models, feminist perspectives, intersectional frameworks) on the development and psychological experiences of men/masculinity. This course also discusses psychological experiences and outcomes of men and masculinity as they relate to topics such as mental and physica

subject: WGSS
title: Black Women Writers
description: Study of black women’s writing from the eighteenth century to the present day. Emphasis will be placed on historical, black feminist, and/or Africana womanist approaches to women’s literature of the African diaspora. Junior or Senior standing or director approval. May be registered as ENGL 4440. Credit not allowed in both ENGL 4440 and WGSS 4440.

subject: WGSS
title: Major American Figures
description: A reading course in the works of a major American writer or writers. Writers to be studied will be specified in the schedule of classes. Maximum credit 6 hours for the degree. On demand. May be registered as ENGL 4270R only when the content focuses on female authors.

subject: WGSS
title: Fiction, Fashion and Feminism
description: An examination of how garments, styles, and fabric function in literary texts. Prerequisites: ENGL 1020 or Department Head approval (program head for the WGSS section). May be registered as ENGL 4500 . Credit not allowed in both ENGL 4500 and WGSS 4500.

subject: WGSS
title: Psychology of Women
description: Analysis of empirical data and theoretical viewpoints concerning the psychological development of women. Psychological effects of sex roles, achievement motivation, and abilities of women; models of socialization practices, personality development, and stages of adjustment. Fall semester. Prerequisites: 6 hours of psychology and or Department Head approval. Junior standing. May be registered as PS

subject: WGSS
title: Topics in Women, Gender and Sexuality Studies
description: Specific topics, themes and subjects related to women, gender and sexuality studies. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL 1010 or ENGL 1011 or UHON 1010 or Department Head approval.

subject: WGSS
title: Women and Textiles
description: A study of women’s role in textile production as laborers, master crafters, consumers, and artists. Prerequisites: ENGL 1010 or Department Head approval.

subject: WGSS
title: Ecofeminism
description: The study of the intersection of feminist issues and environmental issues. Prerequisites: ENGL 1010 or ENGL 1011 or UHON 1010 or Department Head approval.

subject: WGSS
title: Feminist Literary Criticism
description: The history, theory and practice of feminist literary criticism studied in cultural context. Prerequisites: ENGL 1010 or ENGL 1011 or UHON 1010 or Department Head approval. May be registered as ENGL 4710 . No credit in both ENGL 4710 and WGSS 4710.

subject: WGSS
title: Feminist Theory
description: A history of feminist theory from the eighteenth century to the present. Extensive reading, papers. Maybe registered as HUM 4830 or PHIL 4830 . Credit allowed in only one of the three courses.

subject: WGSS
title: Women’s Rhetoric
description: A theoretical, historical, and, primarily, rhetorical examination of women’s discourse through the study of speeches, essays, and other rhetorical artifacts. Special attention will be given to the ways women have used traditional rhetorical strategies and how they have subverted this tradition and/or brought strategies from private life to bear on public discourses. On demand. Prerequisites: ENGL

subject: WGSS
title: Queer Theory
description: A theoretical, historical, and textual look at the intersection of discourses of sexuality and literary and rhetorical analysis. Emphasis will be placed on understanding a broad history and narrative of queer politics and culture. Spring semester. May be registered as ENGL 4885 . No credit in both WGSS 4885 and ENGL 4885 .

subject: WGSS
title: Women’s Studies Internship
description: 120-150 hours of hands-on experience with an appropriate company agency or nonprofit. Students must apply for the internship during the semester prior to that of the intended internship experience. Prerequisites: 15 hours of WGSS courses and approval of Director of Women, Gender and Sexuality Studies and a 3.0 overall GPA and a 2.5 overall GPA.

subject: WGSS
title: Senior Seminar
description: Senior seminar for women’s studies majors that comprises directed readings, presentations, and discussions that will inform a supervised research paper or a service learning project appropriate to the student’s area of interest and experience. Prerequisites: approval of coordinator or Department Head approval. Senior standing.

subject: WGSS
title: Departmental Thesis
description: A two-semester research or creative project resulting in a thesis under the supervision of a faculty member and with the approval of the Honors College. On demand. Prerequisites: Student must coordinate with Honors College to submit a Thesis Contract to get registered for this course. Restricted to Sophomore standing or higher.

subject: WGSS
title: Research
description: Department may have additional prerequisite requirements. Student must submit an Individual Studies/Research Contract to the Registrar’s Office at the time of registration. Every semester. Prerequisites: Department Head approval.

subject: WGSS
title: Individual Studies
description: Enables students to study selected topics in depth. On demand. Prerequisites: Student must coordinate with a specific faculty member to complete the Individual Studies contract to get registered for the course. Restricted to Sophomore standing or higher.

subject: WGSS
title: Group Studies
description: Department may have additional prerequisite requirements. On demand.
